USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain the current posture — keep the Section 301 tariffs (~$250B of Chinese imports, with the $200B List 3 scheduled to rise from 10% to 25% on Jan 1, 2019) on the table as leverage, while preparing to engage seriously at the Trump–Xi G20 meeting in Buenos Aires in late November. Do not push to full 25% prematurely and do not pre-commit to concessions; hold firm, let China make the first substantive move, and be ready to trade a rollback only for verifiable concessions on IP, forced technology transfer, and import purchases.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is modestly favorable (-0.3), not existential. US macro data show no material damage yet: industrial production ~104, consumer sentiment 98.6, Fed funds 2.19% with the fed still hiking, and the broad dollar index at 114.2 — the US economy is absorbing the escalation, and the US holds the offensive (timeline: List 1-3 deployed; China retaliating on only ~$60B, i.e., asymmetric exposure favoring the US). This is opportunity terrain per the USA anchors. However, costs are accumulating and argue against over-escalation: China's ~$60B retaliation including US soybeans pressures the farm belt ahead of the Nov 6 midterms, retail/consumer import-price effects are emerging (Dollar Tree commentary), and October has seen equity and credit volatility (Baa spread widening to ~5.07) tied to trade uncertainty. The action stance (hold, -0.05) reflects that the escalation is already scheduled and needs no new action to preserve leverage, while the confirmed Trump-Xi G-20 meeting (Reuters/WSJ, Oct 11; Kudlow: 'talks have to be serious') creates a genuine off-ramp — but only if talks are serious and yield concrete commitment, which China has not yet offered ('rather unsatisfactory' per Kudlow). Pushing to full 25% now would risk a sharper Chinese response and more market/farm pain with midterms days away; conceding early would waste hard-won leverage before the leaders meet. Hold, negotiate hard at Buenos Aires, and require verifiable commitments before any rollback.
key_factors: US tariffs now cover ~$250B of Chinese imports; $200B List 3 at 10% scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019
China retaliated against ~$60B of US goods including soybeans, pressuring the US farm belt before Nov 6 midterms
US macro robust (Fed funds 2.19%, IP ~104, consumer sentiment 98.6, broad dollar 114.2) — no material GDP damage yet
Trump-Xi G20 Buenos Aires meeting confirmed Oct 11-12; Kudlow: talks must be 'serious'; China offers so far 'unsatisfactory'
October market volatility and widening Baa spreads signal rising cost of over-escalation

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should keep the door open to talks and avoid further tit-for-tat escalation, seeking to freeze or mitigate the scheduled January 2019 rise of List 3 tariffs from 10% to 25%. We have already retaliated proportionally ($34B + $16B + $60B), so we need not escalate again to save face; the priority now is to arrest a trade spiral that is already dragging down our export hubs and currency while preserving a firm negotiating posture. Engage Washington at senior level without new concessions, signaling willingness to increase purchases in exchange for pausing the January escalator, while preparing targeted retaliation if talks fail.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high (not yet existential). US Section 301 coverage has reached ~$250B of our exports across Lists 1/2/3 (timeline 2018-06-15, 2018-07-10, 2018-09-17, 2018-09-24), now roughly half our bilateral exports, and List 3 is threatened to rise from 10% to 25% in January — a material, imminent drag. Real-economy signs confirm the bite: Reuters polling (2018-10-16) forecast Q3 GDP at 6.6%, the weakest since 2009; manufacturing PMI stalled with export orders falling the most in over two years (CNBC 2018-10-01); Guangdong, our largest export province, reported lower exports in the first eight months; and the yuan has lost ~6% against the dollar, testing 7.0 with capital-outflow risk (Reuters/SCMP). Firm-level targeting (the ZTE denial order, timeline 2018-04-16) signals what a broader entity-list campaign could do to our tech sector, reinforcing the +0.6 reading just above the 'major export sectors hit / FX pressure / firm-level targeting' anchor — but not +1.0, since growth remains near the ~6.5% target, PBOC has cut RRR four times and has more room, reserves/controls are intact, and we have matched retaliation at each step.

The action stance is de-escalation-leaning negotiation rather than revenge. Escalating further would hand Washington the pretext to raise List 3 to 25% and broaden beyond $250B, worsening the export and currency damage our macro data already shows; a full capitulation, by contrast, would embolden further demands and erode domestic legitimacy. Negotiating to freeze the January escalator — while keeping retaliatory options ready — is the strategy that both limits self-harm and preserves leverage, hence action_score +0.1 and 'negotiate'.
